abstract.p: This study presents a case of undiagnosed HIV presenting with Kaposi sarcoma (KS) of the head and neck with acute upper airway obstruction (UAO) and provides an updated scoping literature review to examine the patient characteristics, lesion characteristics, interventions, and outcomes of KS cases with UAO from the pharynx, larynx, and/or trachea.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is a highly vascularized neoplasm of endothelial cells, associated with herpesvirus‐8 (HHV‐8). Four subtypes exist: epidemic (human immunodeficiency virus [HIV]/acquired immunodeficiency syndrome [AIDS]‐associated), classic (Mediterranean/Eastern European), endemic (Sub‐Saharan Africa), and iatrogenic (immunocompromised, not AIDS‐associated) [1]. KS classically presents with painless, violaceous mucocutaneous lesions of the skin and oral cavity. KS also commonly involves the gastrointestinal tract, respiratory tract, and lymph nodes. HHV‐8 has been implicated in primary effusion lymphoma, multicentric Castleman disease, and recently described HHV‐8‐related inflammatory cytokine syndrome [2, 3]. Head and neck (H&N) involvement in the United States (US) was rare before the 1980s AIDS epidemic. KS incidence has decreased since, however, reports of laryngeal KS have increased [4, 5]. Treatment options for laryngeal KS include surgical or laser resection, radiotherapy, and/or chemotherapy. KS of the upper airway (UA) risks life‐threatening obstruction and/or hemorrhage. These cases require expedience and decisive management. Due to the relative rarity of H&N KS, standard management guidelines have yet to be established. This study describes a case of undiagnosed HIV presenting with KS‐induced upper airway obstruction (UAO) and provides a scoping literature review examining patient characteristics, lesion characteristics, interventions, and outcomes of KS cases with UAO from the pharynx, larynx, and/or trachea.

sec.title: Case Report
sec.p: A 42‐year‐old male patient presented to a community hospital with 4 months of progressive dyspnea, dysphonia, dysphagia, throat/ear pain, and weight loss. A pharyngeal mass was identified on laryngoscopy, and he was subsequently transferred to a quaternary care center. Physical examination revealed a firm, violaceous lesion of the right posterior tongue and left posterior tonsillar pillar with UAO symptoms. Flexible laryngoscopy identified a friable mass involving the pharyngeal walls, epiglottis, vallecula, false vocal cords, and pyriform sinuses (Figure 1). Contrasted computed tomography imaging demonstrated an enhancing lesion of the left oropharynx extending along the bilateral pharyngeal walls to the hypopharynx and epiglottis (Figure 2). Due to progressive dyspnea and UAO, the patient was urgently taken to the operating room for tracheostomy followed by laryngoscopy with biopsies. Specimens were consistent with KS, and subsequent HIV tests were positive. HIV viral load was 1.1 million copies/mL and CD4 count was 69 cells/mm3. The patient started chemotherapy with doxorubicin and antiretroviral therapy (ART) with dolutegravir and emtricitabine/tenofovir. Decannulation occurred 2 months post‐operatively, given significant symptomatic improvement and mass reduction. At two‐and‐a‐half years post‐tracheostomy, the patient had no lesion recurrence, dyspnea, dysphagia, or pain.

sec.title: Scoping Review
sec.p: A scoping review was conducted on PubMed, with the most recent search on October 2, 2024. Keywords included: “airway obstruction,” “dyspnea,” “respiratory insufficiency,” “sarcoma, Kaposi,” “herpesvirus 8, human,” “laryngeal neoplasms,” “pharyngeal neoplasms,” “tracheal neoplasms.” Articles reviewed were restricted to English without other format restrictions. Cases of KS of the UA with UAO were included, while other sites or absent UAO were excluded. Screening was conducted using Covidence systematic review software (Veritas Health Innovation, Melbourne, Australia), yielding 18 case reports, one retrospective case series, and one non‐controlled trial (Figure 3). Of these 20 articles, 21 patients with KS‐induced UAO were identified (Table 1).

caption.p: Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta‐Analyses (PRISMA) flow diagram of identified, screened, and included studies from the scoping review.

sec.p: Five (24%) cases were published before 1995. Four (24%) had been published since 2020. Most cases described epidemic‐type KS (n = 13, 62%) involving the larynx (n = 17, 81%) in men (n = 15, 71%) with an average age of 43 ± 21 years. Dyspnea and hoarseness were common presentations, with KS diagnosed upon laryngoscopy with biopsies. Sixteen (76%) patients required tracheostomy, with two (10%) deaths from procedure‐related airway hemorrhage. An additional patient (5%) died from hemoptysis at 3 weeks post‐tracheostomy. No other mechanical airway‐related mortalities were reported. Of the remaining tracheostomized patients, seven (54%) were successfully decannulated within a year; four (31%) lacked follow‐up information. Patients were treated with chemotherapy (24%), radiation (14%), laser surgery (14%), microsurgery (10%), or a combination of these (19%) (Table 2). Of the patients with long‐term follow‐up (n = 11, 67%), five (45%) were alive. Mortalities included three (27%) opportunistic infections, one (9%) systemic visceral disease, one (9%) pulmonary embolism, and one (9%) “other cause” at an average of 14 months after presentation.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Presented are 22 cases of KS‐associated UAO. To date, this is the first study to summarize the literature on KS‐associated UAO.

Despite decreased burden of AIDS in the US, H&N involvement of KS, albeit rare, is ongoing [4, 5, 6]. In the most recent systematic review of laryngeal KS, most (85%) patients identified by Barron et al. [4] were after 1995. Similarly, including the presented case, this review of KS‐induced UAO identified 17 (77%) cases after 1995.

The case report patient was found to have epidemic (HIV/AIDS‐associated) KS, which was the most common subtype across the presented literature review (n = 13, 68%). The primary presenting symptoms of the presented case were voice changes and dyspnea, which were also the most common among reviewed cases (n = 12, 63% and n = 10, 47%, respectively). These were also the most common presenting symptoms found by Baron et al. [4] among cases of laryngeal KS.

Skin lesions are a recognizable sign of KS. However, the case report patient presented without characteristic skin lesions or previous positive HIV serology. In a recent literature review, Micali et al. [7] described 13 cases of pulmonary KS without mucocutaneous lesions, seven of which were not known previously to have HIV. Similarly, the current literature review identified five (24%) patients presenting without skin lesions and eight (38%) without previous HIV diagnosis.

KS with UAO is potentially life‐threatening. Similar to the case reported, the presented literature review demonstrates emergency tracheostomy in most patients (n = 16, 76%). Furthermore, just as most other cases in the literature (n = 7, 58%), the case report patient was successfully decannulated within 1 year. Establishing an emergent airway was not without complications. Greenberg et al. and Roy et al. present two cases (9%) of death from tracheostomy‐related airway hemorrhage. Preparations should be made to control potential intraoperative hemorrhaging while managing KS. Depending on lesion location, tracheostomy may contribute to airway hemorrhage and mortality. Cricothyrotomy has been suggested as an alternative in some cases [8]. Careful review of imaging studies and laryngoscopic examination, when available, should guide the approach.

While no definitive guidelines exist for treatment of H&N KS, monotherapy or combinations of chemotherapy, radiation, surgery, or laser excision have been described. The presented case was treated with chemotherapy alone, as were most other cases in this review (n = 5, 24%). These results track with Barron et al. [4] who found that most cases of laryngeal KS were treated with chemotherapy alone. Many case reports lacked patient follow‐up (n = 7, 32%). Unlike the presented patient, who was disease‐free and asymptomatic at 2.5 years, many patients in the literature review died from KS‐related complications (n = 8, 36%).

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: H&N KS is a rare but potentially deadly disease due to its propensity for acute UAO. Despite the continued improvement in HIV care, cases of KS‐induced UAO continue to be documented today. A thorough history and exam are warranted in individuals presenting with UAO, especially in the absence of readily identifiable etiologies. KS should be considered even in the absence of characteristic skin lesions or previous HIV diagnosis. Management may necessitate early tracheostomy with preparation for potential intraoperative hemorrhage. A multidisciplinary approach may be used for local and systemic treatment of KS and underlying conditions (e.g., HIV/AIDS). Even today, providers should be aware of the diagnosis and management of KS‐related UAO.
